title: The great persecution (303)
hookLine: Diocletian orders churches destroyed and scriptures burned

cards: At first light, soldiers and officials force open the doors of a church. It stands in Nicomedia, the city where the emperor Diocletian keeps his court, and the emperors watch from the palace.
Inside, the officials search for an image of God and find none. They find the scriptures, and burn them. They take what they want.

Then the guard comes in with axes and tools, and in a few hours the building is flat. The writer Lactantius tells it this way. It's the opening scene of what Christians came to call the great persecution.

teach.b: First, the order. Lactantius says an edict came out the next day. Christians lost their rank and their protection under the law.
Eusebius, the historian, says the imperial letters ordered churches torn down to their foundations and the scriptures destroyed by fire. Second, the fire in the square.
Eusebius writes that he saw it with his own eyes: houses of prayer thrown down, and the holy scriptures burned in the middle of the marketplaces. Not a rumor. A thing he watched.
Third, the people who said no. In a town in North Africa, the officials came to Bishop Felix and demanded the church's books.

teach.h: I HAVE THEM. I WON'T GIVE THEM.
teach.b: The account of his trial gives his answer, simply: I have them, but I won't give them up. He was put to death for it. Others hid the books, or handed over something else in their place.
Fourth, the people who said yes. Some clergy did hand the books over to save their lives.
Christians in North Africa called them traditores, those who handed over, and the arguments about whether they could still serve as priests and bishops ran on long after the danger was gone.
It's an uncomfortable part of the story, and an honest one: courage and fear in the same churches. Tradition places Agnes, from yesterday, in this same storm.

how: Catholics honor the martyrs of this persecution in the Church's calendar, and the Church still asks the faithful to pray for Christians who suffer for their faith today.

games.q: you're Felix, a bishop in a small African town. officials demand the church's books. what do you say?
o: I have them, but I won't give them up.
games.why: the account of his trial gives exactly that answer. he kept the books, and he was put to death for it.

practice: If there's a Bible or a prayer book near you, put your hand on it, or picture one on a shelf, and notice how ordinary it is to own it.

Then think of people for whom it isn't ordinary: keeping a few pages hidden, reading at night, sharing a single copy with friends, afraid of a knock at the door. If you pray, ask for a safe place for them to read.
